505.title: Ahalya restored
505.hook: an empty hermitage on the road to Mithila, and the woman nobody can see
505.howItsDone: Ahalya is honored in Hindu tradition as one of the panchakanya, five women whose names some Hindus recite in a well-known morning verse; her story is told very differently across tellings, and discussions of it often turn on those differences.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maricha hurled over the sea, alive, and a sacrifice completed. Your line was a way to walk off whole.

With the sacrifice done, the hermits at Siddhashrama have a plan. King Janaka of Mithila is holding a great sacrifice, they tell Rama, and he keeps a bow there you should see. So they walk north for days, and every evening the sage tells stories: how the Ganga came down from heaven, how the ocean was churned. Just outside Mithila, they pass an old hermitage. Lovely, but completely empty. No smoke from the fire, no voices. Whose was this, Rama asks, and why is no one here?
screen: `NORTH, TOWARD MITHILA.` → `STORIES EVERY EVENING.` → `AN EMPTY HERMITAGE.`

segments.voice: This was the hermitage of the great sage Gautama, Vishvamitra tells him, and his wife Ahalya. One day, while Gautama was away, Indra, king of the gods, came to Ahalya disguised as her husband and asked her to be with him. Here the versions part, and it matters which you're hearing. In Valmiki's telling, Ahalya sees through the disguise. She knows it's Indra, and she agrees, the text says, out of curiosity about the king of the gods. Some later tellings say she was fully deceived, and never knew. Either way, Gautama comes home and sees Indra slipping out, still wearing the sage's own form, and in his fury he curses them both. Indra is cursed and humiliated. And to Ahalya, Gautama says: you will stay here for thousands of years, unseen by any living being, living on air, lying in ash, doing penance. Then comes the part that's easy to miss. When Rama comes to this forest and you welcome him as a guest, you'll be free, and return to me in your own form. Gautama leaves for the Himalaya. So the empty hermitage isn't empty at all. Someone has been there the whole time, unseen, waiting for a guest. Go in, Vishvamitra tells Rama. Help her. Tomorrow, what happens when he does.
screen: `GAUTAMA'S HERMITAGE, EMPTY.` · `INDRA IN DISGUISE.` · `THE VERSIONS PART.` · `THE CURSE, AND ITS END.` · then, large: `UNSEEN, WAITING FOR A GUEST.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who might feel unseen: someone quietly carrying something, or left out, or paying a long time for a mistake. Don't judge their story; just picture them, and on each breath out let a little warmth go their way, the way you'd look up and really see someone.
Ahalya restored. Gautama's wife, cursed to live unseen in an empty hermitage until Rama comes and she welcomes him as a guest.
Your line: unseen, waiting for a guest. Her freedom will come through an act of welcome. Until tomorrow.

506.title: Ahalya restored
506.hook: she isn't stone, and she isn't only rescued: in Valmiki, she is the host
506.howItsDone: In much of popular Hindu tradition, Ahalya is freed from stone by the touch of Rama's foot, a scene loved for what it says about Rama's grace; Valmiki's version, where she is invisible and freed by hosting him, is often taught alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ahalya restored, part one: an empty hermitage, a curse, and someone unseen there for years. Your line was unseen, waiting for a guest.

On television, in comic books, from a grandmother's lap, the scene usually goes like this. A stone lies by the path. Rama's foot brushes it, and the stone becomes a woman. It's a beautiful picture, and an old one. But it isn't Valmiki's. In Valmiki's Sanskrit there's no stone at all, and no foot brushing against one. What happens instead is quieter, in some ways more striking, and it starts with a woman nobody can see.
screen: `A STONE BY THE PATH.` → `RAMA'S FOOT TOUCHES IT.` → `NOT IN VALMIKI.`

segments.voice: Rama walks into the hermitage, with Vishvamitra and Lakshmana behind him, and there she is. Ahalya, shining with the power of her long penance, the text says, but hidden: like a flame wrapped in smoke, like the moon behind a cloud, like sunlight dazzling on water, so bright you can't quite look at it. Until now, no one could see her at all. Now Rama sees her, and the curse is over. Then the brothers take hold of Ahalya's feet, the respect you'd show an elder. Two princes bow to a woman the world has looked away from for years. Ahalya remembers Gautama's words and does exactly what the curse said would free her: she receives them as guests. She brings water to wash their feet, offers welcome, honors them as a host honors guests. Flowers fall from the sky. Drums sound in heaven. Gautama returns and is reunited with her, and together they honor Rama. Look at the shape of it. She isn't lifted out of a rock by a foot. She's seen, she's honored, and she acts. The one being rescued is also the one offering hospitality. In the tellings where she becomes stone, the scene says something about Rama's grace. In Valmiki, it also says something about her: after all those years, she's still a host.
screen: `A FLAME WRAPPED IN SMOKE.` · `THE PRINCES TOUCH HER FEET.` · `SHE RECEIVES THEM AS GUESTS.` · `GAUTAMA RETURNS.` · then, large: `SEEN, HONORED, AND HOSTING.`

segments.voice: Picture someone you care about arriving at your door, and imagine opening it, offering a glass of water, saying welcome. Feel what it's like to give, even on a day you yourself feel tired or overlooked, and let that small act of welcome be enough.
Ahalya restored. Seen at last by Rama, honored by the princes, and freed as she welcomes them as guests, then reunited with Gautama.
Your line: seen, honored, and hosting. Next, the city with the bow. Day five hundred six, done.

507.title: Janaka's bow
507.hook: a priest asks about his mother, and a king tells where his bow, and his daughter, came from
507.howItsDone: Hindus celebrate Sita's appearance from the earth on Sita Navami, in the month of Vaishakha, and Mithila, in today's Bihar and Nepal's Janakpur region, holds her as its own daughter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ahalya restored, part two: no stone in Valmiki, but a woman unseen, freed by being seen and by hosting her guests. Your line was seen, honored, and hosting.

The travelers reach Mithila, and King Janaka comes out to receive them with his priests. One is Shatananda, Janaka's chief priest. His first question to Vishvamitra isn't about the bow, or the princes, or the sacrifice. Did you show my mother to Rama? Was she honored? Did my father come back to her? Shatananda is Ahalya and Gautama's eldest son. Yesterday's story was his family's. And when he hears yes, she's free, they're together, he's overjoyed. Then the king speaks of something else.
screen: `MITHILA, AND ITS PRIEST.` → `DID YOU SHOW MY MOTHER TO RAMA?` → `YES. SHE'S FREE.`

segments.voice: These boys would like to see the bow, Vishvamitra says, and Janaka tells its story. Long ago, at the great sacrifice of Daksha, Shiva was refused his share of the offerings. In anger he raised this very bow against the gods, ready to cut them down. The gods begged him to relent; he did, and gave them the bow. The gods gave it to Devarata, an ancestor of Janaka's line, to keep, and it has stayed in Mithila ever since. A bow that once threatened the gods. Then Janaka tells a second story, about his daughter. Once, he says, I was plowing a field to prepare for a sacrifice, and out of the furrow the plow had cut, a girl rose up. I raised her as my own and named her Sita. Sita means furrow, the line a plow cuts. She wasn't born from a womb, the text says; she came from the earth itself. That's why she's often called Bhumija, daughter of the earth, and Janaki, daughter of Janaka. So in one speech the king sets two things side by side: a bow of Shiva, kept for generations, and a daughter of the soil, raised with love. And he's decided that only the one who can handle the first can marry the second. Tomorrow, what that has cost him.
screen: `SHATANANDA, AHALYA'S SON.` · `SHIVA'S BOW, RAISED AT DAKSHA'S RITE.` · `KEPT BY JANAKA'S LINE.` · `SITA RISES FROM THE FURROW.` · then, large: `SĪTĀ: THE FURROW.`

segments.voice: Feel the ground beneath you, the floor, the foundation, the earth under that, and let your weight sink into it, held by it and fed by it the way Sita was. Breathe in and feel the earth support you; breathe out and give your weight back to it.

508.title: Janaka's bow
508.hook: kings who couldn't lift it decided to take Mithila instead
508.howItsDone: Across India, the contest of the bow is staged in Ramlila performances; later retellings such as the Ramcharitmanas present it as a swayamvara, while Valmiki describes Sita as viryashulka, won by strength.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shiva's bow from Daksha's sacrifice, and Sita rising from the furrow. Your line was Sita rising from the furrow.

Janaka made a decision about his daughter, and he announced it. Sita, he said, is viryashulka: the price of her hand is strength. Not gold, not alliances, not land. Whoever can lift and string Shiva's bow may marry her. Word spread. Kings came from everywhere to try, and every one of them failed. Then, Janaka tells Vishvamitra, something ugly happened. Wounded pride doesn't always go home quietly. Sometimes it comes back with an army.
screen: `THE PRICE OF HER HAND: STRENGTH.` → `KINGS COME FROM EVERYWHERE.` → `EVERY ONE OF THEM FAILS.`

segments.voice: The kings who failed were furious, insulted by a bow. They joined forces and laid siege to Mithila. For a whole year the city was surrounded, and supplies ran low. Janaka, who couldn't match their armies, turned to austerity and prayer, and the gods answered him with an army of their own. The kings were scattered and fled. So when Janaka shows Rama the bow, it's no party trick. It's a test that has already cost his city a war, and he knows what happens when proud men fail it. If Rama can string this bow, Janaka says, I'll give him Sita. Then he orders it brought out, and Valmiki makes the scene huge. The bow lies in an iron chest on a cart with eight wheels, and the text says it takes five thousand tall, strong men to haul it in, with great effort. They set it down before the king and the guests. Think about what Rama is looking at. Not just weight. A bow a god once aimed at the gods. A line of kings who failed and turned to violence. A father who will give his daughter only for real strength. And the whole hall, waiting to see what the young prince will do.

509.title: Janaka's bow
509.hook: a bow no king could lift, picked up as if it were nothing, and the sound that follows
509.howItsDone: The breaking of the bow is a high point of Ramlila performances and Ramayana recitations; in many places audiences cheer as the bow snaps, and the scene is often painted and sung at weddings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: strength as the bride-price, kings who failed and besieged Mithila, and a cart hauled by thousands. Your line was strength as the bride-price.

The chest is open. The bow lies there, enormous. Nobody in the hall speaks. Vishvamitra looks at Rama and says one short line: Rama, my son, look at the bow. No speech. Rama steps forward and asks, politely: may I touch it? May I try to lift it, and string it? The king and the sage both say yes. And then, in front of thousands of people, something happens that Valmiki tells in only a few verses.
screen: `THE CHEST IS OPEN.` → `RAMA, MY SON, LOOK AT THE BOW.` → `MAY I TOUCH IT?`

segments.voice: Rama takes hold of the bow in the middle and lifts it, the text says, as if in play: the bow thousands of men just dragged in on a cart, the one a line of kings couldn't budge. He bends it and strings it. He draws the string back, all the way to his ear. And with a crack like thunder, the bow breaks in two. The earth shakes like a mountain splitting. Everyone in the hall falls to the ground, stunned, except four: Vishvamitra, King Janaka, Rama and Lakshmana. Notice a few things. Rama asks permission before touching it; he doesn't grab at it the way the angry kings would have. He lifts it lightly, so the strength isn't a strain for him. And he doesn't set out to break it. He draws it fully, the way a bow is meant to be drawn, and it can't hold him. Notice too who stays standing: the teacher, the father, the one who drew it, and the brother who never leaves his side. When the people come to, Janaka is full of joy. I've seen Rama's strength with my own eyes. Sita will bring glory to our family by marrying him. My promise is fulfilled. He asks Vishvamitra's leave to send fast messengers to Ayodhya, to bring Dasharatha. The bow is broken. The wedding is coming.

510.title: the four weddings
510.hook: one wedding becomes four, and two families tell their whole histories first
510.howItsDone: Hindu wedding rites include naming the gotra and ancestors of the bride's and groom's families, a custom echoed in Vasishtha's and Janaka's recitations in the Ramayana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama asked first, lifted the bow as if in play, and it broke like thunder. Your line was the bow breaks in two.

Janaka's messengers ride hard to Ayodhya. They stand before Dasharatha, the king who not long ago begged a sage not to take his young son. Your Rama broke Shiva's bow, they tell him. Your Lakshmana is with him, safe. King Janaka asks you to come to Mithila for the wedding. You can imagine the old man's face. The next morning Dasharatha sets out with Vasishtha, his priests, his army and his treasure. When the two kings meet, Janaka welcomes him like family before they are family.
screen: `MESSENGERS RIDE TO AYODHYA.` → `YOUR RAMA BROKE SHIVA'S BOW.` → `TWO KINGS EMBRACE.`

segments.voice: Before anyone marries, the families recite their family trees, aloud, all the way back. Vasishtha names the line of Ikshvaku, generation after generation: from Brahma, through Manu, Ikshvaku himself, kings like Sagara, whose sons dug deep into the earth, and Bhagiratha, who brought the Ganga down from heaven, all the way to Dasharatha. Then Janaka names his own line from King Nimi down, including Devarata, who received the bow. Why? Because in this world a wedding isn't two people meeting. It's two long stories joining. Then Janaka makes the formal gift: Sita to Rama, and his second daughter, Urmila, to Lakshmana. And then a lovely thing happens. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha together suggest something more. Janaka's younger brother, Kushadhvaja, has two daughters too, Mandavi and Shrutakirti. Why not give them to Bharata and Shatrughna? Janaka agrees with joy. So one wedding becomes four: four brothers, four sisters and cousins, two royal houses woven together in a single day. Before the ceremony, Dasharatha gives away an enormous gift of cows in his sons' names, and a final guest arrives: Yudhajit, Bharata's uncle from Kaikeyi's family. From now on, whatever happens in Ayodhya happens to Mithila too.

511.howItsDone: In Hindu weddings, the kanyadana, the father's giving of the bride's hand, and the circling of the sacred fire are central rites; some families recall Janaka's words to Rama when they explain them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two family trees recited aloud, and one wedding became four. Your line was one wedding becomes four.

If you've been to a Hindu wedding, you may know the moment, though customs vary from family to family. The fire is lit in the middle of the canopy. The priest is chanting. The bride's father stands, takes his daughter's hand, and places it in the groom's hand. Rooms full of noisy relatives go quiet for it. That moment has an echo in the Ramayana. Janaka, the king who found his daughter in a furrow, brings Sita to the altar, decked in jewels, and stands her across from Rama, by the fire.
screen: `THE FIRE UNDER THE CANOPY.` → `A FATHER, A HAND, A HAND.` → `JANAKA BRINGS SITA TO THE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: Janaka speaks to Rama: iyam sita mama suta sahadharmachari tava. This is Sita, my daughter, your companion in dharma. Accept her. Take her hand in yours. She will be devoted to you, and follow you always, like your shadow. He pours sacred water, and the gods say well done. Sahadharmachari is the key word. Saha, together. Dharma, the right way, duty, the path. Chari, one who walks. One who walks the path of dharma together with you. Not a possession, not a prize, though she was won by strength: a companion on the way. Janaka gives Urmila to Lakshmana, and his brother's daughters to Bharata and Shatrughna, with similar words. Then the four couples circle the fire three times, keeping it on their right. Flowers fall from the sky, heavenly drums sound, and the apsaras dance. The next morning Vishvamitra says goodbye and leaves for the northern mountains. The sage who took two boys from their father's house leaves them married, with their father and brothers around them. Now the week, from the top. An empty hermitage, and Indra's disguise. Ahalya seen, honored, and hosting. Shatananda's question, and Sita rising from the furrow. The siege of the failed kings. The bow breaking like thunder. Two family trees recited. And today, four couples circling one fire.
